site_or_subject: Google / Alphabet global operations (data centers and offices), Scope 2 electricity emissions (2024, 2025)
record: Alphabet's schedules reviewed by Ernst & Young LLP at limited assurance give Scope 2 location-based emissions of 15,148,700 tCO2e and market-based emissions of 2,815,000 tCO2e for 2025 (report dated 22 June 2026), a difference of 12,333,700 t, and 11,283,200 tCO2e and 3,059,100 tCO2e for 2024 (report dated 16 June 2025, in Google's 2025 report, p.112), a difference of 8,224,100 t. For 2025 they give 43,586,600 MWh of electricity consumption, attributed to 'PPAs and other renewable energy agreements' (32,986,300 MWh), on-site generation (24,800 MWh) and renewable electricity in the grid (10,575,500 MWh), and class 7,282,000 MWh of purchased electricity as from non-renewable sources. For 2024: 32,179,900 MWh (data centers 30,825,600 MWh), split 24,504,500, 20,500 and 7,654,900 MWh across the same three lines, with 8,110,400 MWh non-renewable.
claim: "we again matched 100% of our electricity consumption with renewable energy purchases" (ninth consecutive year); 24/7 carbon-free energy ambition. Google's 2025 report (p.101) says that to reach the 100% it first counts on-site generation and the renewable electricity already in the grids it uses, then buys contractual instruments, including surplus renewable electricity in other regions where it cannot source enough locally. Google reports an hourly carbon-free energy share of 66% across its data centers and offices for 2024 (2025 report, p.107); ESG Dive reports approximately 65% for 2025 and contracted removals of 1.38 million tons [press: ESG Dive].
gap: Market-based Scope 2 was 2,815,000 t against 15,148,700 t location-based in 2025 (81.4% lower) and 3,059,100 t against 11,283,200 t in 2024 (72.9% lower). The market-based method replaces grid-average emission factors with the company's contractual instruments and residual-mix factors; the location-based figure is the grids'. Whether 2024 was restated in the 2026 report is not shown (Google states a 3% fall in market-based Scope 2 for 2025; the assured values give 8.0%). Google's own hourly carbon-free share (66% in 2024) is the only hourly figure in the seven operators' documents read here.
verification_note: The 2025 Scope 2 figures and the electricity split were read in EY's FY2025 review report and its Appendix A schedules and re-read directly on 2026-10-23 (see scope2-renewable-claims-by-instrument). 2026-10-24: Google's 2025 Environmental Report was read from a browser download; it prints EY's FY2024 review report (limited assurance, dated 16 June 2025, p.112) and its Appendix A schedules (pp.112-114), which give the 2024 Scope 2 values, electricity consumption and renewable split; the values equal those in the report's data tables (pp.105, 107) and the Internet Policy Review tabulation, which is dropped as a source. The hourly CFE share is not in the reviewed schedules and stays a claim. The 2026 report's data tables (pp.69-109) were not read, so a restatement of 2024 is not checked, and the 2025 hourly CFE share was not read in a primary source.

site_or_subject: NSW state-significant data-centre approvals and Sydney potable water use
operator: NSW Department of Planning; Sydney Water; AirTrunk, Amazon, Microsoft, Goodman (Road 1)
record: NSW Planning confirmed to Reuters (Sep 2025) that all 10 data-centre applications ruled on since 2021 were approved [press: Reuters]. Sydney Water's own answers to the NSW Legislative Council data-centres inquiry (received 22 Jun 2026) give 26 smaller data centres approved and connected, 101 servicing requests (75 larger facilities totalling ~250 ML/day), seven planning agreements for 74 ML/day, and average-day demand of ~110 ML/day by 2030 and ~260 ML/day by 2035 if all requests proceed, against ~1,500 ML/day supplied across Greater Sydney, and attribute the 15-25% range to other submissions citing Sydney Water; the ledger converts the 2035 figure to about 95 GL/yr (260 ML/day x 365), roughly 17% of supply (260 / 1,500). NSW's only water standard is that the government be 'satisfied that the development contains measures designed to minimise the consumption of potable water'. The NSW Planning Portal lists Road 1 Data Centre (SSD-80814238, Macquarie Park, 34.3 MW) as approved 1 Oct 2026 with a Sydney Water Growth Data Form attached but no public water volume.
claim: Per Reuters (Sep 2025), the 10 approved applications carry A$6.6bn of construction spending and project up to 9.6 GL/yr of potable water (~2% of Sydney's maximum supply), totals of the applicants' figures that NSW Planning confirmed; Sydney Water told Reuters that data centres could use up to 135 GL (a quarter of available water) by 2035. Reuters describes an AirTrunk 320 MW facility (no source named) whose planning documents say rainwater harvesting cuts potable use by 0.4%, and two Amazon centres whose documents give 195.2 MW and up to 92 ML/yr of drinking water before rainwater harvesting. AirTrunk says 'subsequent modelling recently tabled to Sydney Water has determined actual usage will be significantly lower' than planning figures; Amazon says its Australian sites avoid water cooling 95.5% of the year.
gap: Planning-stage water projections (up to 9.6 GL/yr) differ from operators' later 'significantly lower' modelling, and Sydney Water's 2035 forecast to the inquiry (~260 ML/day, about 95 GL/yr if all requests proceed) differs from the 135 GL Reuters attributes to it; Sydney Water says it relies on proponents' forecasts, IPART notes its pricing proposal did not include data-centre demand or servicing costs, and NSW imposes no numeric water-use reporting requirement, so no record of actual consumption was found yet.
verification_note: Partial (2026-10-22): Sydney Water's 22 Jun 2026 answers to the NSW LC data-centres inquiry give 26 connected, 101 requests, ~110 ML/day (2030) and ~260 ML/day (2035) vs ~1,500 ML/day supply and do not state 135 GL or 25% (earlier record attributed 135 GL/a quarter to Sydney Water); IPART's 27 Mar 2026 submission cites a preliminary Sydney Water estimate of up to 250 ML/day by 2035. SSD-80814238 (34.3 MW) approval 2026-10-01 confirmed earlier on the Planning Portal. Still press-only: NSW Planning's 10 approvals/A$6.6bn/9.6 GL, AirTrunk 320 MW and Amazon 195.2 MW/92 ML figures (not in the Premier's Department answers; hearing transcripts truncated in fetch; legislation.nsw.gov.au returned errors for the potable-water clause). Third pass (2026-10-24): the applicants' totals (A$6.6bn, 9.6 GL, ~2%), Sydney Water's 135 GL remark to Reuters and the AirTrunk and Amazon site figures moved to claim (the site figures are Reuters' reading of applicants' documents); the 95 GL/yr and 17% are the ledger's conversions, now basis derived with formulas; the unsourced Ryde council moratorium was removed from the gap.

site_or_subject: Scala AI City
record: MME Portaria SNTEP/MME nº 2.942 (9 May 2025) recognised Scala Data Centers S.A.'s access alternative to the Rede Básica for the Eldorado do Sul data center (sectioning of the 525 kV Guaíba 3–Nova Santa Rita C1 line, ~2.34 km of double-circuit 525 kV extensions and a new 525/230 kV Scala DC substation) as least-global-cost and compatible with expansion planning. The Portaria states no MW amount, makes effective connection conditional on an ONS Parecer de Acesso, ANEEL authorisation and ONS-verified system availability, and lapses if the installations are not in a transmission-use contract (CUST) by 31 Dec 2033. The municipality's enabling law makes licensing 'simplificada e autodeclaratória'; Rio Grande do Sul has no environmental licensing category for data centers (Fepam proposed one, no timeline). The municipality (39,559 residents, IBGE 2022 census) was flooded in May 2024 [press: Agência Brasil]; Brasil de Fato reports the project site itself was not flooded [press: Brasil de Fato].
claim: Scala says Scala AI City will reach 4.75 GW at full build on a 10 million m² site over 10 to 20 years, with a first phase of BRL 3 bn and 54 MW of IT capacity [press: Intelligent CIO, Jornal do Comércio]. site_or_subject: Data Center Pecém (Casa dos Ventos; ByteDance reported client)
record: ANEEL vetoed the connection in April 2025 on ONS advice citing transmission overload risk; ONS access opinions were reported on 29-30 May 2025, and ANEEL's authorisation for Data Center Pecém II (500 kV, future SE Pecém III) was published in the DOU on 26 Jun 2025 [press: O Povo, DCD]. ONS letter CTA-ONS DGL 0815/2026 (8 Jun 2026) records that ANEEL Despacho 914/2026 granted Casa dos Ventos a precautionary measure keeping priority and capacity reserve for Data Center Pecém II. Semace licensed phase 1 on a Relatório Ambiental Simplificado (RAS), classed low-impact; two SRH water-use permits were issued, and an 18 Aug 2025 Cipp S/A–Utilitas reuse-water agreement replaced initially planned artesian wells [press: O Povo]. An MPF technical report (Laudo 1308/2025, Dec 2025) is reported to find that the licença prévia indicates 30 m³/day of groundwater while the SRH permits allow 88.24 m³/day [press: O Povo]. On 22 Oct 2025 Idec, the Anacé people, Terramar and Frei Tito asked the MPF to suspend licensing and annul the licença prévia, citing lack of EIA/Rima and ILO 169 consultation [press: O Povo]. On 10 Sep 2026 the MPF and DPU filed Ação Civil Pública nº 0080626-66.2026.4.05.8100 against builder Omnia and Semace (State of Ceará and Caucaia later added), stating that the licença prévia and licença de instalação had been granted on an RAS, citing 300 MW installed power, ~70 ha and 120 diesel generators, and seeking to bar the operating licence and energisation pending ILO 169 consultation of the Anacé, an EIA/Rima and groundwater pumping tests.
claim: Casa dos Ventos says the project will run on 100% renewable energy from new dedicated plants and that licences rest on detailed technical studies. The developer's RAS (658 pages, as reported by O Povo, 22 Oct 2025) identifies 31 impacts, 10 significant (3 positive, 7 negative), projects a phase-1 average draw of 210 MW (5,040 MWh/day) and water use of 18–30 m³/day via closed-loop air-cooled chillers (O Povo attributes 30 m³/day to Casa dos Ventos and the RAS; the 18 m³/day has no named source). Reuters, as relayed by DCD (2 Jun 2025), reported an initial 300 MW scalable up to 900 MW; Casa dos Ventos said operations were slated for January 2027. Semace says all legal procedures were followed, community hearings are a condition of the installation licence, and the permitted groundwater volume is a ceiling, not actual use [press: O Povo].

site_or_subject: SQM lithium brine extraction: SMA sanction and compliance program

Minería Chilena links the program to the Primer Tribunal Ambiental's ruling in case R-21-2019 [press: Minería Chilena], but that ruling (27 Oct 2020) concerns another procedure: it rejected a claim by the Aymara community of Quillagua and the Quechua community of Huatacondo against SMA Res. site_or_subject: Energy Efficiency Act (EnEfG) data-centre PUE, heat-reuse and renewable obligations
record: EnEfG § 11 (statute text): data centres commissioned from 1 July 2026 must reach an energy usage effectiveness (PUE) <= 1.2 within two years of commissioning and a share of reused energy of at least 10% (planned 15% from 1 July 2027 and 20% from 1 July 2028; DIN EN 50600-4-6, with listed exemptions); existing data centres must reach PUE <= 1.5 from 1 July 2027 and <= 1.3 from 1 July 2030; electricity use must be covered on a balance-sheet basis by renewable electricity at 50% from 1 Jan 2024 and 100% from 1 Jan 2027; operators must also report to the Energieeffizienzregister fuer Rechenzentren (per the TUV summary). A government bill amending the EnEfG was still in draft when the Bundesrat gave its opinion on 10 July 2026 (BR-Drs. 388/26). Mainova (30 June 2026) reports Frankfurt's daily peak load exceeded 900 MW on 25-26 June 2026, up from clearly above 850 MW a year earlier, with grid capacity expected to more than double; the release does not attribute the load to data centres.
claim: none found
gap: Statutory numeric heat-reuse targets exist, but no public aggregate from the national register showing compliance with the 1 July 2026 threshold was located.

record: The Commission's first technical report (EY, Borderstep and AIT for DG ENER, July 2025) on the 2024 reporting period under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364 covers 770 reporting data centres, about 36% of estimated EU data centres; six member states had no reported data and five had fewer than three. Germany reported the most sites (335 of an estimated 456), followed by France (133) and the Netherlands (85); Czechia reported none of an estimated 50 and Ireland 18 of an estimated 123 (15%). The report gives per-site means rather than EU totals: renewable energy about 16.8 GWh; guarantees of origin about 12.5 GWh, PPAs about 5.3 GWh (median 0; the report flags a possible unit misinterpretation) and on-site generation about 0.04 GWh. The three component means are taken over different subsets of sites and sum to about 17.8 GWh, more than the total; as shares of that sum they are roughly 70% / 30% / 0.2% (derived). WUE could be computed for 458 sites and a non-zero ERF for only 67. The Commission's public dashboard (last updated 25 Sep 2026), read for its 'reporting period 2025' view, shows 773 data centres in 11 countries, total energy consumption of 20.7 TWh, 4.4 GW of installed IT power demand and 8,752,919 m³ of water input, with weighted averages of PUE 1.27, WUE 0.51, REF 0.84 and ERF 0.0236; by size band, very large data centres (90) average a PUE of 1.19 and very small ones (143) 1.52. DG ENER's data-centre page states that a report on the 2025 period is under preparation, that the Commission proposed a common rating scheme on 21 Sept 2026, and that publication of its proposal on minimum performance standards is planned for Q2 2027.

site_or_subject: GHG Protocol Scope 2 Guidance (2015) and its revision: dual reporting, Scope 2 Quality Criteria, hourly matching and deliverability proposals
operator: GHG Protocol (WRI / WBCSD); Independent Standards Board (ISB); Scope 2 Technical Working Group
record: The GHG Protocol Scope 2 Guidance (2015) states that "companies shall report scope 2 according to a location-based method and a market-based method" (Executive Summary, s.5.1); the full Guidance (s.3.2, p.11) applies this to operations in "markets with choice in electricity product or supplier". All contractual instruments used in the market-based method "shall" meet the Scope 2 Quality Criteria, among them: "Be tracked and redeemed, retired, or canceled by or on behalf of the reporting entity", "Be issued and redeemed as close as possible to the period of energy consumption", and "Be sourced from the same market in which the reporting entity's electricity-consuming operations are located" (Executive Summary, Table 1, p.6). A Scope 2 Technical Working Group of 45 experts was convened from September 2024. The public consultation on proposed revisions opened on 20 October 2025, was scheduled to close on 19 December 2025, and was "extended to January 31, 2026". The GHG Protocol release named "a new hourly matching and deliverability requirement for market-based reporting" as "a central feature of the proposal", together with load profiles, exemption thresholds, a phased timeline and "a legacy clause for existing contractual commitments"; the consultation slides also proposed using "the most precise location-based emission factor accessible". The feedback summary of 29 July 2026 reports "nearly 1100 responses from 56 countries" and states that "The proposals for hourly matching and deliverability showed low levels of support", while feasibility measures and a legacy clause for existing long-term contracts "received broad support". In July 2026, "ISB members indicated majority support for the idea of developing two marketbased methods": Method 1 would "incorporate hourly matching, deliverability and incrementality" requirements and Method 2 would "maintain existing scope 2 requirements from the 2015 Scope 2 Guidance". The proposed direction is that companies "should report using Method 1 until a to-be-determined date" and "may report using Method 2"; after that date they "shall report using Method 1 if data that meets the quality criteria is available". As of the GHG Protocol update dated 16 October 2026, the revision is not final: a "consolidated public consultation" is "slated for Q2 2027" and the joint GHG Protocol-ISO Corporate Standard is "slated for publication in Q4 2028". No effective date has been published; the 2015 Guidance remains the operative text.
claim: The GHG Protocol says of its proposal: "The proposed revisions also introduce several measures to improve the implementation feasibility of the updates."
gap: Under the 2015 Guidance still in force, annually matched certificates from the same market reduce market-based Scope 2; the hourly matching and deliverability revision is not final and has no effective date as of October 2026.
verification_note: All quotes are from GHG Protocol documents fetched on 2026-10-23. The full 2015 Guidance PDF could not be read past about p.43, so the Quality Criteria are quoted from the official Executive Summary (Table 1); the dual-reporting rule was confirmed in the full Guidance (s.3.2 p.11; s.7.2 p.32). The October 2026 update PDF's filename is dated 20261006, and the document reads as dated 16 October 2026. The feedback summary gives no support percentages per proposal. Exemption threshold values, load-profile rules and legacy-clause cut-off dates were not stated in the documents read. The 16 October 2026 status page was re-read directly on 2026-10-23. The GHG Protocol is a private standard-setter, not a record holder; its documents are recorded here as what its own rules say (basis standard_or_methodology), as in sbti-netzero-scope2.

site_or_subject: Johor Data Centre Development Coordination Committee approvals, rejections and Tier 1/2 halt
operator: Johor State Government (DCDCC; Special Technical Committee)
record: Johor's committee (formally the Jawatankuasa Pembangunan Pusat Data Negeri Johor, JPPDNJ, which screens applications for zoning, infrastructure, water, electricity and buffer zones before they reach local authorities, under a state data-centre planning guideline approved in April 2024) began vetting applications in June 2024. In a 28 Nov 2024 state-assembly answer the Menteri Besar stated data centres must meet PUE not above 1.5 and WUE of 1.8; on 20 Nov 2025 exco Mohd Jafni Md Shukor told the assembly WUE must be below 1.8 under the planning guideline, with approval priority for applicants not using Syarikat Air Johor (SAJ) water. The state reported 42 approved projects to Q2 2025 and, in a Nov 2025 written answer, 17 operating data centres. The NST (19 Nov 2024) reports that the committee rejected nearly 30% of applications in five months and, per its vice-chairman Lee Ting Han, 4 of 14 foreign-operator bids, citing failure to show sustainable water/energy practices and sites lacking utility infrastructure; it gives Johor capacity as 10 MW in 2021 and ~1.3 GW in Nov 2024 [press, source not named for the 30% and capacity figures: New Straits Times]. The NST (27 Nov 2025) reports 51 approved projects (17 operational, 11 under construction and 23 at the approval stage) and that the state 'will no longer approve' Tier 1 and Tier 2 facilities, which it says can use up to 50 million litres/day versus ~200,000 L/day for Tier 3/4; data centres needing water must use reclaimed water rather than SAJ supply [press, source not named: New Straits Times].
claim: Johor state media give RM164.45bn of investment for the 42 approved projects. Market research firm Baxtel projects Johor capacity of 2.7 GW by 2027 (as quoted by the NST, 19 Nov 2024). Johor state says its vetting ensures 'digital growth cannot come at the cost of taps running dry for households' and that Bridge Data Centres and Computility Technology were directed to use treated recycled sewage water.
gap: Approved-project counts (42 to Q2 2025 per state media; 51 by Nov 2025 per press) and capacity figures (1.3 GW in press; 1.6 GW cited by ISEAS) are not in a single state register; the ~30% rejection rate and the Tier 1/2 halt appear only in press, and no JPPDNJ decisions or the planning guideline text are public.
verification_note: Partial (2026-10-22): Dewan Negeri Johor papers confirm the JPPDNJ committee and April 2024 planning guideline (27 Nov 2024), PUE <=1.5 and WUE 1.8 (28 Nov 2024, MB) and WUE <1.8 (20 Nov 2025, Jafni), and 17 operating data centres (Nov 2025 written B26); Media Digital Johor confirms 42 approvals to Q2 2025. Earlier record dated the WUE 1.8 threshold to Jan 2026; it was stated in the assembly by Nov 2024. Not found in assembly papers (Nov 2024 and Nov 2025 oral/written sets, Nov 2025 Penyata Rasmi excerpt) or state media: the ~30% rejection, 51-project and Tier 1/2 halt figures. Third pass (2026-10-24): the NST gives the ~30% rejection rate, the 10 MW and ~1.3 GW capacity figures and the 51/17/11/23 counts in its own voice (only 4 of 14 is attributed to the vice-chairman), so they are marked as press with no source named; the 2.7 GW projection is Baxtel's, not the official's, and the RM164.45bn investment value is the state's statement, both now in claim; '23 unbuilt' is now the article's '23 have received approval'.

site_or_subject: Lagos data centers: on-site diesel and gas generation
record: NERC's 2025 Q4 report lists 11 captive generation permits (136.19MW in total) granted that quarter, none to the Lagos data-centre operators checked (Rack Centre, MainOne/Equinix, OADC, Kasi, Digital Realty/Medallion, Africa Data Centres); earlier quarters' tables were not read. No TCN, LASERC or Lagos State record of data-centre power sourcing was found. TechCabal (4 Nov 2025), in its own reporting and without naming sources, puts diesel at about ₦1,000/L and estimates that a 1 MW diesel-backed load burns about 270 L/h (about ₦275,400/h at ₦1,020/L); it says gas is typically 30–60% cheaper, energy is over 35% of Nigerian data-centre opex, and the grid struggles to deliver a stable 5,000 MW [press, own estimates: TechCabal].
claim: In an interview on 28 Oct 2025 (TechCabal), Rack Centre CEO Lars Johannisson described a 'hybrid energy strategy' of gas generation and solar to reduce reliance on diesel, tied to a new 12 MW expansion, and put the sector's installed base at about 25 MW, growing to 180–200 MW; Rack Centre says it continues to build gas generation and solar as part of its energy mix; CEO: 'Energy is the elephant in the room' and 'I don't think there's any policy slowing development'. Rack Centre's March 2025 media briefing (company-sourced Techpoint 'Brand Press' post) describes its 12 MW LGS2 data centre as running on 'predominantly gas power, diesel and eventually solar', with gas turbines installed to complement diesel generators. Connecting Africa (Jun 2025) counts 17 data centers, 14 in Lagos, from the DataCenterMap directory, and cites a Mordor Intelligence market estimate of ~136.7 MW for 2025. MTN reported 40% power savings from gas versus diesel (per Connecting Africa, Jun 2025; no primary source).
gap: No NERC, TCN or Lagos State record of data-centre power sourcing or generator permits found yet (NERC's 2025 Q4 permits include none for the operators checked; earlier quarters not read); the cost and fuel figures are TechCabal's own estimates, and the sector capacity figures differ (CEO about 25 MW installed base; Mordor Intelligence ~136.7 MW for 2025).
verification_note: Searched NERC permit records and Lagos State sources for data-center generation permits or fuel use; found only press reports of NERC generation permits to other firms (including MTN), none tied to a data center. No primary document located; figures remain operator statements (TechCabal) and a market estimate (Connecting Africa). Second pass (2026-10-22): re-read both sources. TechCabal states the diesel price, 270 L/h, ₦275,400/h, 30-60% gas discount, >35% opex share and 5,000 MW grid figure in its own voice, not as the CEO's words. The record previously attributed all these figures to the CEO and stated a diesel/gas mix for LG2; both are corrected. NERC orders and permit registers were not searched in this pass. Third pass (2026-10-22, follow-up): found Rack Centre's own March 2025 briefing (Techpoint 'Brand Press', company-sourced). It describes LGS2 power as 'predominantly gas power, diesel and eventually solar' with gas turbines complementing diesel generators, so the LGS2 gas/diesel mix removed in the second pass is restored with this attribution. site_or_subject: Microsoft Middenmeer (Agriport) drinking-water use and AMS13/14 permit
record: The Tweede Kamer adopted a motion on 4 Oct 2022 (Kamerstuk 26 643, nr. 919) recording that Microsoft's Wieringermeer data centre used 84 million litres of drinking water for cooling in 2021 against Microsoft's earlier estimate of 12 to 20 million litres, and asking the government to consider a ban or at least a cap on drinking-water use as a permit requirement for hyperscale data centres. The municipal permit documents retrieved (2020 Nota van zienswijzen for AMS13/14) contain no drinking-water volume. The province's data-centre strategy 2025-2027 records that PWN now gives drinking-water connections only for office use. No PWN or municipal meter reading for the site was found yet.
claim: Microsoft gave a drinking-water figure of 12-20 million litres a year in June 2021, which the municipal executive repeated to residents [press: Noordhollands Dagblad]. In April 2022 Microsoft reported to the municipality 84 million litres used in 2021 (75 million operations, 9 million facilities), and the municipality changed the figures on its website [press: Computer Weekly, Data Center Dynamics]. Documents released under a Wob request contained an estimate above 100,000 m3 a year by an engineering firm hired by Microsoft [press: Noordhollands Dagblad]. Microsoft said the 12-20 million figure described use at that time (per Noordhollands Dagblad) or the fully operational phase (per Data Center Dynamics), that the 2021 volume included construction water, that a mature site is on track for about 10 million litres a year, and that 36 million litres were discharged back, leaving net consumption near 48 million litres [press]. Its 2023 fact sheet gives a WUE of 0.08 L/kWh for 2022.
gap: The 2021 volume Microsoft reported to the municipality (84 million litres) is 4.2 to 7 times the 12-20 million litre figure (84/20 and 84/12), and Microsoft's net figure (48 million litres) is 2.4 to 4 times it (48/20 and 48/12). No PWN or municipal meter reading was found yet, and the municipal document carrying the 84 million litres is not online, so every volume rests on press reports of Microsoft's figures.
verification_note: Read 2026-10-24: the adopted motion (Kamerstuk 26 643, nr. 919, 4 Oct 2022) records the 84 million litres used in 2021 and Microsoft's earlier 12 to 20 million litre estimate, and asks the government to consider a ban or cap on drinking-water use for hyperscale permits; the Nota van zienswijzen and the provincial strategy 2025-2027 were read for the Middenmeer receipt. Every water volume is Microsoft's own figure known through press (Data Center Dynamics, Noordhollands Dagblad, Computer Weekly) and now sits in claim; the record holds no volume of its own. Data Center Dynamics reports Microsoft calling the 12-20 million figure the fully operational estimate, while Noordhollands Dagblad reports 'then-current use'; both are given. Hollands Kroon's portals, the municipal Wob documents and archived web pages could not be read, so no municipal or PWN figure is on record.

site_or_subject: Meta hyperscale campus Zeewolde (cancelled) and national hyperscale siting rule
record: [older: 2022] On 10 June 2022 the cabinet approved a draft decree (in force 1 January 2024, Stb. 2023, 492, per the Middenmeer receipt) barring municipalities from permitting new hyperscale data centres except in two areas: the former Eemsmond part of Het Hogeland and the Agriport A7/B1 sites in Hollands Kroon; the draft decree (2023 text, Barro art. 2.15.1) defines hyperscale as more than 10 ha and 70 MW or more, and exempts applications made on or before the 16 Feb 2022 voorbereidingsbesluit. The cabinet said the rule did not apply to Zeewolde, where the zoning plan had already been adopted, but that the Rijksvastgoedbedrijf could not sell the state land to the municipality, citing a TNO assessment that some conditions were not met. The Eerste Kamer had adopted a motion on 21 Dec 2021 (35925 XIV, H) asking the government to have the Rijksvastgoedbedrijf suspend sales of agricultural land for hyperscale data centres.
claim: Meta's planned campus (five data halls, 200 MW at full build, as reported by Data Center Dynamics) was cancelled by July 2022; Meta stated that building in Zeewolde 'is not the right investment' and that its siting priority is 'a good match with the environment'.
gap: The draft national rule did not apply to Zeewolde, whose procedures had started; the state did not sell the required land, and Meta cancelled its project. The record is from 2022; no later reversal was found.
verification_note: Rijksoverheid release (2022-06-10), the 2023 draft decree (>10 ha, >=70 MW; 16 Feb 2022 cut-off) and the Eerste Kamer motion dossier confirm the rule and the land-sale position; the exemption covers two specific areas rather than whole municipalities, the rule expressly did not cover Zeewolde, and the confirmed Senate motion is 35925 XIV H of 21 Dec 2021. A 'March 2022 Senate motion' reported by press was not found and has been dropped (2026-10-24). Meta's 200 MW, five-hall plan and the cancellation are Meta's own account via Data Center Dynamics and sit in claim. See also nl-zeewolde-meta-land (same Zeewolde case).

site_or_subject: Meta hyperscale datacenter, Zeewolde: state land sale
record: The Meta site included land of which the State owned 'a large part' (Council of State, 2023); NOS put the State share at about 80 ha [press, source not named: NOS]. The Eerste Kamer adopted a motion on 21 Dec 2021 (35925 XIV, H) asking the government to have the Rijksvastgoedbedrijf suspend sales of agricultural land for hyperscale datacenters. In the 22 Feb 2022 Senate interpellation the minister said the State still held the land as a private-law party but would not undo the municipal permit. Minister De Jonge's letter of 10 June 2022 (Kamerstuk 26 643 nr. 862) transmitted TNO's assessment of the municipality's plan against the Aug 2021 sale conditions. The same day the Rijksvastgoedbedrijf wrote to Zeewolde that it could not sell the land on the current assessment. TNO found the design energy-efficient for now, with intelligent cooling and no drinking water used for cooling, but roofs, facades and surrounding land not maximally used for solar, rainwater use unclear and the residual-heat plan too undeveloped to assess. On 20 Sep 2023 the Council of State annulled the Trekkersveld IV zoning plan (ECLI:NL:RVS:2023:3550), noting that neither the municipality nor the initiator owned the land and that there was no certainty the State would sell.
claim: Senator Koffeman (PvdD) gave the site as 166 ha, a figure NOS also gives without a source, and stated in the 22 Feb 2022 Senate interpellation that only about 15% of residual heat could be used. Meta declined to comment on the June 2022 decision; it had earlier paused the project after both parliamentary chambers opposed it.
gap: Parliamentary, ministerial and Rijksvastgoedbedrijf records document the sale conditions, TNO's findings and the refusal to sell, and the zoning plan was annulled in 2023; the State's share of the land is given in hectares only by NOS (the Council of State says 'a large part'), and the ~15% heat-reuse figure is a senator's statement. Older sources (2022-2023).
verification_note: Second pass: fetched the Rijksvastgoedbedrijf letter to Zeewolde of 10 Jun 2022 (Eerste Kamer copy), the Rijksoverheid release of the same day and the minister's 13 Jun 2022 letter to the Senate, which confirm the non-sale decision and TNO's mixed findings on solar, rainwater, cooling and residual heat; the Council of State ruling of 20 Sep 2023 (ECLI:NL:RVS:2023:3550) confirms that the State owned 'a large part' of the land but gives no hectares. The ~80 ha State share is still only in NOS (none of the RVB letter, the 13 Jun letter, the motion, the interpellation record or the ruling states it). Correction: the ~15% residual-heat figure was stated by Senator Koffeman in the interpellation, not recorded as a finding, and the 166 ha is also his figure. See also nl-zeewolde-meta-cancelled (same Zeewolde case). 2026-10-24: the 166 ha and ~15% figures moved to claim as Senator Koffeman's statements; NOS's ~80 ha, given without a source, is marked as such.

site_or_subject: Proposed temporary prohibition on new data centres mainly engaged in cryptocurrency mining

record: The Storting energy and environment committee's recommendation Innst. 280 S (2024-2025), dated 6 May 2025, on representative proposal Dok. 8:112 S (which asked to 'utrede et permanent forbud mot utvinning av kryptovaluta i Norge' - investigate a permanent ban on crypto mining in Norway) recommends that the proposal '- vedtas ikke.' site_or_subject: Statnett reserved grid capacity for data centres in northern Norway

site_or_subject: SBTi Corporate Net-Zero Standard V2.0: Scope 2 target basis and market-based instrument criteria
record: The SBTi Corporate Net-Zero Standard Version 2.0 was released on 11 June 2026, with an effective date of 1 February 2027 (version history); earlier consultation drafts were published in March 2025 and November 2025. Criterion CNZS-C9.4 states that companies "shall determine target ambition based on the physical GHG inventory, including the location-based method for scope 2". Near-term Scope 2 targets may be absolute reduction targets or low-carbon electricity (LCE) alignment targets "to increase the percentage of LCE used, contracted, or matched on a linear trajectory" (C12.2.a). On instruments, the Standard states "Contracts for plants up to 15 years of age are allowed" and "Existing contracts will be grandfathered for the duration of the contract" (A.5, p.9); activity pools are "defined on the basis of deliverability regions"; a PPA may cover load across pools in one synchronous grid where "the offtake begins within 36 months of the project's commissioning" (C30.3.b); default-delivered LCE counts where "LCE accounts for at least 95% of the generation mix" (C31.1). Hourly matching is not required for target progress: SBTi describes an annual requirement with matching "within a maximum 12-month period", and companies with significant consumption are "required to report the share of electricity consumption matched with low-carbon electricity on an hourly basis". The criteria document sets hourly reporting for pools of 10 GWh or more (C32.1) and voluntary recognition thresholds of 'at least 50% hourly matching' until 2030, at least 75% until 2035 and at least 90% from 2035 (C34.1). SBTi says exceptions guidance will be "published by Q4 2026" and that it "intends to launch a Call for Evidence on hourly matching".
claim: SBTi states: "The intention is that SBTi aligns with the GHG Protocol's direction of travel on scope 2, without pre-empting the outcome of the GHG Protocol's ongoing work."
gap: SBTi V2.0 sets Scope 2 target ambition on the location-based inventory and limits instruments by plant age and deliverability, but requires annual, not hourly, matching for target progress; it applies from 1 February 2027.
verification_note: Release and effective dates, C9.4, the 15-year rule and grandfathering were read in the full Standard PDF. Section 4 of the full Standard could not be read, so C12.2.a, C30.3.b and C31.1 are quoted from the Criteria PDF. C32.1 ('where total annual electricity consumption is 10 GWh or more') and C34.1 ('Until 2030: at least 50% hourly matching', 'Until 2035: at least 75% hourly matching', 'From 2035: at least 90% hourly matching') were re-read verbatim in the Criteria PDF on 2026-10-24. The annual 12-month matching and Category A hourly-reporting points are quoted from the SBTi blog. SBTi is a private standard-setter; its standard is treated here as a record of its own rules.

site_or_subject: Mandatory disclosure rules on Scope 2: EU ESRS E1, ISSB IFRS S2, California SB 253, US SEC climate rule
operator: European Commission / EFRAG; ISSB (IFRS Foundation); California Air Resources Board (CARB); US Securities and Exchange Commission
record: EU ESRS E1 (Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772): EFRAG's Q&A (ID 831, 31 October 2024) cites E1 AR 45(d), which requires undertakings to "apply the location-based and market-based methods to calculate Scope 2 GHG emissions"; the text of E1-6 paragraph 49 itself was not reached. EFRAG's July 2025 draft amended E1 (v1.6, an unapproved working document) keeps paragraph 32(b): "Scope 2 GHG emissions (location-based and market-based)". EFRAG reported on 3 July 2026 that the European Commission had published the delegated act on revised ESRS; EFRAG states the revised standards "will apply to financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2027", subject to Parliament and Council scrutiny; the adopted revised E1 text was not read. ISSB IFRS S2: paragraph 29(a)(v), as reproduced in an AASB staff paper (21 May 2024), requires an entity to "disclose its location-based Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions" and "provide information about any contractual instruments that is necessary to inform users' understanding"; B31 says the entity "might disclose information about its market-based Scope 2". The ISSB's December 2025 amendments (effective for periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027) changed 29(a)(ii), Category 15, GWP and industry-classification rules; 29(a)(v) was not amended. California SB 253: CARB approved the Initial Regulation at its February 2026 meeting, setting a first deadline of 10 August 2026 for a report that "will include only Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions" for entities with "more than $1 billion in annual revenue"; CARB's program page now states the deadline "is November 10, 2026", with the regulation applying "if approved by the Office of Administrative Law". CARB pages read do not state the Scope 2 method; CARB's 21 July 2026 workshop proposed, as summarised by Ropes & Gray (not confirmed in a CARB document), that Scope 2 be "calculated and reported using both market-based and location-based methods" under "the current 2015 version of the Scope 2 Guidance", with limited assurance from 2027. US SEC: the March 2024 climate rules were stayed on 4 April 2024; the Eighth Circuit held the challenges in abeyance on 12 September 2025; on 29 May 2026 the SEC proposed "to rescind the climate disclosure rules in their entirety" (Release No. 33-11421). No final rescission was found as of 23 October 2026.
claim: none found
gap: ESRS E1 requires both location-based and market-based Scope 2; IFRS S2 requires only location-based plus information on contractual instruments; SB 253's Scope 2 method awaits CARB rulemaking; the SEC rule never took effect and is proposed for rescission.
verification_note: The verbatim text of ESRS E1-6 paragraph 49 (Set 1) was not reached: EUR-Lex and mirror texts of Regulation 2023/2772 could not be read as far as ESRS E1. site_or_subject: Server/AI hardware depreciation lives in SEC filings vs circularity claims
record: Amazon's SEC filings: servers' useful life 3 to 4 years from 1 Jan 2020, then 4 to 5 years and networking equipment 5 to 6 years from 1 Jan 2022 (Q1-2022 depreciation -USD 973 m; full year 2022 -USD 3.6 bn, with a USD 2.8 bn benefit to net loss), servers 5 to 6 years from 1 Jan 2024 (Q1-2024 -USD 897 m, net income +USD 695 m; full year 2024 -USD 3.2 bn, net income +USD 2.5 bn), then 'a subset of our servers and networking equipment' cut from 6 to 5 years from 1 Jan 2025 due to 'the increased pace of technology development, particularly in the area of artificial intelligence and machine learning' (Q1-2025 depreciation +USD 217 m, net income -USD 162 m, 'primarily impacted our AWS segment'; for the full year 2025 the 10-K gives depreciation +USD 1.4 bn and net income -USD 1.0 bn, or USD 0.10 per share); in Q4 2024 Amazon also retired certain servers and networking equipment early, recording about USD 920 m of accelerated depreciation, for the same stated reason. Alphabet extended servers from 4 to 6 years and certain network equipment from 5 to 6 years beginning FY2023 (Q1-2023 depreciation -USD 988 m, net income +USD 770 m). Microsoft extended server and network equipment from 4 to 6 years beginning FY2023 (Jul-Sep 2022 operating income +USD 1.1 bn). Meta extended most servers and network assets to 5.5 years from 2025 (Q1-2025 depreciation -USD 826 m). Microsoft's 2025 Environmental Data Fact Sheet shows Deloitte & Touche LLP limited assurance on Section 1 (GHG, energy, water and waste tables, with operational waste tonnages and packaging recyclability but no cloud-hardware reuse/recycle percentage) for FY24, with diverted waste of 28,285 t. No public filing stating a physical lifespan for GPUs, or an assured GPU resale/refurbishment volume, was found.
claim: Amazon's own 10-Ks anticipated that each lengthening would raise operating income in its first year by USD 3.1 bn (2022, per the FY2021 10-K; 2024, per the FY2023 10-K). Google reports UL 2799 Zero-Waste validation at two data centers and one warehouse. Microsoft claims a 92% reuse-and-recycling rate for servers and components in FY25 (90.9% in FY24) and Circular Centers expanded to seven facilities (2026 report), 3.2 million components reused, and more than 2,500 t of packaging diverted from more than 30,000 server racks. Google claims about 8.8 million components harvested for reuse/resale in 2024, more than 7.5 million harvested and 2.6 million resold in 2025 (more than 54 million since 2015), and zero-waste campuses rising from 23% (2022) to 50% (2025). Google reports 84% of data-center operational waste diverted (2024).
gap: Good practice with caveats: Microsoft's FY24 waste tables (including 28,285 t diverted) carry Deloitte limited assurance, but its 90.9% server reuse/recycling figure is not in the assured fact sheet; Google's component counts sit outside EY's FY2025 review scope and UL 2799 covers site waste only; accounting lives of 5-6 years are estimates, and Amazon's 2025 cut and its early retirement of some servers in Q4 2024, both citing AI, are the only filing-level shortenings found (Meta lengthened most server lives to 5.5 years in the same year).
verification_note: Pass 2 (2026-10-22): SEC 10-Q Note 1 text confirms each useful-life change and its quarterly effect: Amazon Q1-2022 (servers 4 to 5, networking 5 to 6 years; -USD 973 m), Q1-2024 (servers 5 to 6; -USD 897 m), Q1-2025 (subset 6 to 5 citing AI/ML; +USD 217 m, NI -USD 162 m, primarily AWS); Alphabet Q1-2023 (4 to 6 / 5 to 6; -USD 988 m, NI +USD 770 m); Microsoft Q1 FY2023 (4 to 6); Meta Q1-2025 (5.5 years; -USD 826 m). site_or_subject: What datacenter generators emitted outside Virginia: EPA National Emissions Inventory 2020 and 2023, facilities classed as computing infrastructure and data processing

site_or_subject: AEP Ohio data center tariff (central Ohio)
record: PUCO opinion and order of 2025-07-09 in Case 24-508-EL-ATA (approved 5–0) adopted the stipulation of AEP Ohio, PUCO Staff, the Ohio Consumers' Counsel and others (rejecting a competing settlement backed by Microsoft, Amazon, Google and the Data Center Coalition) and ordered AEP Ohio to end, as soon as possible, a moratorium on new data center service in place since March 2023. Under the resulting Schedule DCT (effective 2025-07-23), new data centers or expansions of 25 MW or more pay a minimum demand of up to 85% of contract capacity, with a load ramp of no more than four years plus eight years (initial term up to 12 years), an exit fee of 36 months of minimum charges available after the fifth post-ramp year, and collateral of 50% of total minimum charges for customers without qualifying credit; existing facilities grandfathered. AEP Ohio testimony reported inquiries from >50 customers at >90 sites totaling >30 GW, and central Ohio data center load rising from ~100 MW (2020) to ~600 MW (2024) [press: POWER]. PUCO denied rehearing by September 2025 [press: Ohio Capital Journal]; data center industry groups appealed to the Supreme Court of Ohio in November 2025.
claim: PUCO Chair Jenifer French: the order is 'a well-balanced package that safeguards non-data center customers.' AEP Ohio projects central Ohio data center load reaching ~5 GW by 2030 [press: POWER]. Data Center Coalition: 'no one customer type or industry should be singled out for disparate rate treatment.'
gap: Tariff terms are confirmed from AEP Ohio's tariff page and the OCC, but the PUCO order text has not been read yet and AEP's load figures rest on press reporting of its testimony.
verification_note: Pass 2 (2026-10-22): PUCO press release (2025-07-09) confirms the order adopting the AEP/Staff/OCC stipulation and the moratorium end; AEP Ohio's Schedule DCT page confirms 25 MW, 85% maximum minimum demand, ramp of up to 4 years plus 8 years (12-year term) and effective date 2025-07-23; OCC confirms 85% and up to 12 years and the November 2025 Supreme Court appeal. The opinion and order PDF (DIS CMID A1001001A25G09B43531I00509) could not be read, nor could an archived copy, so the order text and AEP's 30 GW / 600 MW / 5 GW figures (Kelso testimony, via POWER) remain unconfirmed from the docket. site_or_subject: Microsoft Mount Pleasant data center and We Energies gas build
record: PSC Wisconsin final decisions dated 2025-07-02 approved, subject to conditions, a 1,100 MW simple-cycle gas plant (five GE 7FA.05 combustion turbines, about $1.205B excl. AFUDC) at the South Oak Creek Facility, 'directly west of the existing Oak Creek Power Plant and Elm Road Generating Station' (docket 6630-CE-317), and a 128 MW, seven-engine RICE plant in Paris, Kenosha County ($279.6M excl. AFUDC; docket 6630-CE-316). In both, finding of fact 6 reads: 'The proposed project is necessary to satisfy the significant probable future requirements of one customer, the Very Large Customer.' The decisions record that We Energies gave the purpose as 'primarily to serve a significant new load source in the Interstate 94 (I-94) corridor', identified in rebuttal as the data center Microsoft is developing in Mount Pleasant (the decision records Phase 1 as announced at 450 MW), and that it intends to serve 'the data center under the Very Large Customer tariff'. The Commission found that evidence 'persuasive that the new load will be realized', wrote that 'when the entirety of a forecasted new load rests on the actions of a single customer, the risk is greater', and ordered the utility to notify it within 30 days if the Very Large Customer's load forecast significantly decreases. A separate 2 Bcf LNG storage facility at Oak Creek ($456.3M excl. AFUDC, docket 6630-CG-140) received a final decision on 2025-09-09, and a 33-mile gas transmission pipeline to supply the Oak Creek and Paris plants (Rochester Lateral, docket 6630-CG-139; the applicant estimated $210,942,310 for Route A or $217,093,529 for Route B) received a PSC final decision on 2025-12-02. The PSC's 2026-05-21 final decision on We Energies' Very Large Customer and Bespoke Resources tariffs (docket 6630-TE-113; Microsoft an intervenor) required a 15-year initial term, made the VLC tariff mandatory for loads of 100 MW or more, and allowed Bespoke Resources outside MISO Local Resource Zone 2 (eastern Wisconsin and Michigan's UP). Microsoft's 15-year service contract for Mount Pleasant, signed as-is on 2026-07-16, still requires supply plants to be in eastern Wisconsin or Michigan's UP [press, source not named: Wisconsin Watch]. We Energies is also seeking to buy Invenergy's proposed Red Oak Ridge gas plant (docket 9837-CE-100, up to 1,186 MW per the PSC case page), with Microsoft already contracted for its output [press: Wisconsin Watch]. The U.S. Department of Energy (Office of Energy Dominance Financing) completed its environmental review on 2026-08-31 for a proposed Title XVII federal loan guarantee to Wisconsin Electric Power Company covering the Oak Creek Combustion Turbine Project: five 220 MW combustion turbines (about 1,100 MW) on a 16-acre parcel within the existing Oak Creek Generating Site, approved by the PSC in July 2025; the letter itself states no purpose.

We Energies says the gas plants are part of an 'all of the above' approach consistent with its 2050 decarbonization goal.

The signed contract's terms rest on a press report that names no source, and the Red Oak Ridge price on a press report of the utility's request.
